title: Term Limits for Congress
resolution: Resolved: The United States should adopt term limits for members of Congress.
summary: Presidents are limited to two terms, but members of Congress can serve as long as voters reelect them. Most Americans say they favor term limits. Would they make Congress better?

background.p: Members of Congress have no term limits. In U.S. Term Limits, Inc. v. Thornton (1995), the Supreme Court held that states cannot impose term limits on their members of Congress; a constitutional amendment would be needed. Proposed amendments in recent Congresses would cap House service at three or six terms and Senate service at two, usually not counting terms already served.

Support for term limits is broad and bipartisan in polls; a 2013 Gallup survey found 75% would vote for them. Fifteen states limit the terms of their own state legislators, generally to between 6 and 12 years, which gives researchers evidence on how limits work in practice. The Congressional Research Service summarizes the main arguments: supporters say turnover makes Congress more responsive; opponents say elections already let voters remove members and that experience keeps power with elected officials rather than staff and lobbyists.

disputed.q: How have state legislative term limits worked?
positions: Supporters point to more turnover and new kinds of candidates.
Several studies find that limits shift influence toward governors, staff and lobbyists because members leave before gaining expertise.

terms.def: A cap on how many terms a person may serve in an office.
The edge sitting officeholders have in elections, from name recognition, fundraising and staff.
The part of the Constitution describing how it can be amended.
Understanding of how an organization works, built over time.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Limits would bring fresh people and ideas into Congress and loosen the grip of long-serving incumbents.

args.claim: Incumbents are very hard to defeat.
args.warrant: Name recognition, fundraising networks and district lines give sitting members large advantages, so elections alone rarely produce turnover.
args.evidence: Reelection rates for House incumbents; research on the incumbency advantage.
args.response: The negative answers that voters reelect members they like, and that high reelection rates reflect choice, not failure.

args.warrant: Members who know they'll return to private life are more likely to think like their constituents and less like career politicians.
args.evidence: CRS summary of arguments for limits; surveys on public trust in Congress.
args.response: The negative replies that members facing a fixed exit may look ahead to lobbying jobs, which can make them less responsive.

args.claim: It would reduce the concentration of power in long-serving members.
args.warrant: Seniority helps decide committee chairs; limits spread leadership among more members and regions.
args.evidence: Histories of seniority and committee power; party rules that already limit chair terms.
args.response: The negative argues that parties already limit chair terms, which addresses this without limiting voters' choices.

args.warrant: When large, bipartisan majorities support a reform for decades, Congress's refusal looks like self-interest.
args.evidence: Gallup (2013) and other polls cited by CRS.
args.response: The negative replies that popularity doesn't show a reform will work, and voters can impose limits themselves by voting members out.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Term limits take choices away from voters and drain Congress of the expertise it needs.

args.warrant: Voters can remove any member at the next election; term limits take away their right to keep a representative they want.
args.evidence: CRS summary of arguments against; the Supreme Court's reasoning in Thornton about voters' choices.
args.response: The affirmative answers that incumbency advantages make elections an imperfect check.

args.claim: Limits shift power to staff, lobbyists and the executive branch.
args.warrant: Lawmaking is complex; members who leave just as they master it leave more of the work to unelected staff, lobbyists and agencies.
args.evidence: Studies of state legislative term limits; the CRS summary.
args.response: The affirmative replies that state results vary and Congress could strengthen its own staff and research offices.

args.warrant: Knowledge of budgets, defense, health policy and the rules of Congress takes years to build; limits throw it away.
args.evidence: Examples of long-serving legislators' work on complex legislation; studies of legislative effectiveness and experience.
args.response: The affirmative answers that a limit of twelve years still allows real expertise to develop.

args.claim: Lame-duck members may be less accountable.
args.warrant: A member in a final term doesn't face voters again, so the electoral check disappears for that term.
args.evidence: Research on behavior of term-limited officials in their last term.
args.response: The affirmative replies that the same is true of second-term presidents, and the benefits outweigh this.

strawmen.strawman: They think everyone in Congress is corrupt.
strawmen.why: Supporters argue about incentives and incumbency advantages, not about every member's character.
strawmen.steelman: Incumbents' advantages make elections a weak check; limits bring turnover and fresh perspectives and reduce concentrated power, as most Americans want.

strawmen.strawman: They want politicians to stay in office forever.
strawmen.why: Opponents trust voters to decide and worry about expertise and lobbyists.
strawmen.steelman: Elections already let voters remove members; limits take away voters' choice and shift power to staff, lobbyists and agencies.

weak.why: Overclaiming; argue about turnover and incentives.
A constitutional amendment would make them constitutional; Thornton only stops states from imposing them alone.

Why can't voters simply vote out members they don't like?

neg: What share of House incumbents win reelection?
Would you support limits on committee chairs instead?
